title: TA9-21603
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: Madam, I have heard your evidence this morning concerning why you cannot return to Sri Lanka and I have reviewed your personal information form and my notes concerning your evidence. I have considered your counsel's submissions and these are the reasons why I reject your claim.

The claimant alleges that when she lived in XXXXX she was targeted by both the LTTE and the security forces of Sri Lanka and she was suspected by the security forces of supporting the LTTE and as a result of that ongoing suspicion and the problems that that caused her she decided that she must flee Sri Lanka and she then moved for a short period of time to XXXXX and she alleges that with the help of an agent she left Sri Lanka using her genuine Sri Lankan passport and national identity card and went to Singapore.

While in Singapore she was provided with a new passport and handed her genuine passport and national identity card to her agent. She used the new passport to travel to Japan and from Japan to Canada, entering Canada by way of Pearson International Airport and two days later made a refugee claim inland in Etobicoke.
She entered Canada on October 5, 2009; two days later made a refugee claim at the Etobicoke office asking for Canada's protection.

The core of this claim is credibility and credibility comes from two basic concerns. The explanation as to how she travelled to Canada, the explanation for the missing genuine Sri Lankan passport and national identity card and there are credibility concerns concerning her total lack of documents to support with one exception, that she was in Sri Lanka at the times she claims. I will deal with that exception later.

First of all, I want to deal with the travel to Canada. The claimant testified that she left Sri Lanka with her genuine passport but was unable to remember the airline that she used for the trip to Singapore. She was provided a passport in Singapore which was fraudulent but she was unable to remember the country that had issued that fraudulent passport. She was unable to remember the airline that she used to travel from Singapore to Japan; she was unable to remember the airline she used to travel from Japan to Canada. She testified that she was never given that passport, that fraudulent passport but the agent used it on her behalf to get boarding passes at Singapore and Japan, to clear exit controls from Singapore, entry controls into Japan, exit controls from Japan and entry controls into Canada.

Counsel has submitted that because she was under the control of the agent she would perhaps not remember details. Counsel also submitted that she was fleeing for her life and her primary concern would be to escape Sri Lanka and she is a woman and it is plausible that she would not remember the airline or some other details about her trip.

If the claimant had forgotten the name of one of the airlines, the details as to how she entered or left one of the countries that might be plausible, but I find it implausible that the claimant would not remember anything of her trip, any of the documents used or how they were used or at what times they were used on her trip to Canada. It is simply implausible that she would travel to Canada on a forged document and not know the country that issued that forged document. It is further implausible that she would not have been told the name of the holder of the forged document. The lack of knowledge of the forged document on its face does not appear to be consistent with the information she gave the immigration officer at question 19 of the schedule 1 on the claim for refugee protection found as part of Exhibit R-2. Since in question 19 she indicated that the country that issued the forged document was Canada. It is further implausible that the agent would be able to hold these documents at all times and not have her in possession of the document when boarding the plane or when going through the various controls at various airports. And so while I agree with counsel that it is plausible that a claimant of this age might not remember some of the details, I do not accept it as plausible that they would not remember any of the details.
Counsel submitted that the claimant came to Canada approximately a year ago. It was actually ... it is a much shorter period than that, after being corrected by counsel, I agree it was 10 months.

So it is ten months since she left Sri Lanka and nine months since she came to Canada, approximately. I asked the claimant a number of questions about documents that she might possibly have that would help her place herself in Sri Lanka when she claims. I certainly would expect no claimant to have all of those documents that I questioned. But again it is equally implausible that a claimant would have none of those documents. They included questions about possible bank records and considering that she sold a house before she left Sri Lanka, records concerning the ownership of the house or the sale of the house, driver's licenses in Sri Lanka are helpful because they are photo identification. They are renewed on a regular basis, but the claimant testified that she never had a driver's license, did not drive, and as a result I have in evidence only two documents that would be helpful in placing her in Sri Lanka at the time she says. I think I stand corrected; I have only one document that places her in Sri Lanka at the time she claims.

The letter from her friend here in Canada mentions 1992; it makes no mention of any knowledge of the claimant being in Sri Lanka after 1992. The birth certificate of course is not photo identification, it has no photo identification. It was obtained in XXXXX 2004 but even that does not place her in Sri Lanka in XXXXX 2004 since it is possible to get a copy of your birth certificate in Sri Lanka without being physically present.

So that leaves the letter from the attorney that I received at the hearing and was printed on XXXXX of either 2000 or 2010, since it has been corrected. It is a form letter and the personal information has been typed on a printed form. When the claimant was asked as to how she knew this attorney she testified that it was her parent's attorney. She was asked when she last met this gentleman in Sri Lanka; she testified that she met him by accident in 2009. She was asked where she met him, she testified first about five miles from her home and after further questioning she remembered that she met him while she was grocery shopping but again she was asked where exactly were you and she testified, in front of the shop. But she had never used this lawyer professionally.

I am satisfied that if this letter was to be given weight and in this case sufficient weight to offset the lack of all of any other evidence that would place her in Sri Lanka, that the claimant would have been clear in her mind where and when she last met this gentleman and that was clearly not the case in her evidence. Further I am satisfied that the date on the letter would ... there would have been no need to correct that date and particularly not correct it by simply adding a one between the last two zeros of the year 2000. Further I am satisfied that an attorney, even if it was a form letter today, would not have had to resort to typing the personal information. As a result I give this letter insufficient weight to offset all of the missing evidence, particularly the passport.

The claimant, when testifying as to the passport, indicated that she gave her original passport to the agent in a house in Singapore with the understanding that he would mail it to an address that she provided him here in Canada. The claimant testified that she kept her birth certificate for the balance of the trip from Singapore. If the reason that the agent was taking the passport and national identity card from the claimant was that she would not be found with conflicting pieces of identity if searched, then there would be no reason why the claimant could not have simply mailed the national identity card and her passport to herself here in Canada, or if not mailed, sent by courier.

Yes, I have heard in other cases agents use genuine passports given by their clients to create fraudulent passports for subsequent clients, but a Sri Lankan passport without a visa would be of little value to the agent who is in the business of moving claimants from Sri Lanka to other countries. The claimant maintains that she kept her birth certificate because she thought she would need it; in reality, either the passport or the national identity card would have much more benefit to the claimant than the birth certificate.

Further, since the agent came with her to Canada and there is no evidence that he did not bring that passport with him to Canada; he would be equally at risk of having two pieces of identity documents if searched when arriving in Canada. On a balance of probability I am satisfied the claimant did not give her passport to an agent in Singapore. Further, I am satisfied the claimant did not travel to Canada on a forged passport since she did not know the name of the holder of the passport or any other details that would have been necessary to use a forged passport. I am satisfied that for some unknown reason the claimant has decided not to divulge her genuine Sri Lankan passport.

The claimant was asked in two areas of her documents for her occupation in Sri Lanka; to the immigration officer and in the Schedule B documents she indicated that she was unemployed, that was consistent with the answer she provided in her Personal Information Form in question 7 and she said it was not applicable. In question 31, in the narrative, paragraph 2, she testified that she owned a grocery store and received an income from it and that was consistent with her oral evidence. When asked to explain why she did not indicate that she was a shop owner or some other such indication in the other two areas she testified that it was only a small shop but she agreed it was her only source of income and so when the question was put directly to her that if you owned a small grocery store why not indicate that in both your personal information form and when you were talking to the immigration officer. Her explanation was that she forgot.

I am satisfied, that on the balance of probabilities, that if the claimant's only source of income in Sri Lanka was as an owner of a small grocery store, that her evidence would be consistent on that point and all parts of her claim and since that is not the case I am satisfied it is more probable than not that she did not own a XXXXX store if she was living in Sri Lanka.

In summary, her evidence as to how she travelled from Sri Lanka to Canada was not credible. Her evidence as to providing the agent with her genuine passport and national identity card so it could be mailed to her later was not credible. Her explanation for having no documents other than the lawyer's letter to support that she was in Sri Lanka at the times after 1992 is implausible. Her answers concerning her employment in Sri Lanka were inconsistent and hence not credible and as a result, on a balance of probability, I find that the claimant was not a credible witness, did not travel to Canada in the way that she described, did not own a XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX and as a result the claimant has failed to establish that there is a serious possibility that she will face persecution due to her ethnicity as a Tamil, born in the north of Sri Lanka or suffer other forms of serious harm.

Hence, the Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim pursuant to both section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
